Reference: Costinot and Rodríguez-Clare (2014); Paper Link

Model Setting

This handbook chapter asks how large the welfare consequences of globalization are, and how the answer depends on the model used to compute it. It organizes the new quantitative trade literature around gravity models: general equilibrium models with constant-elasticity import demand in which bilateral trade flows satisfy a gravity equation. Two tools carry the whole analysis. The first is a sufficient-statistic welfare formula: the change in real consumption caused by a foreign shock can be inferred from the change in the share of expenditure on domestic goods and the trade elasticity. The second is the exact hat algebra popularized by Dekle, Eaton and Kortum (2008): counterfactual changes in trade flows and incomes solve a nonlinear system that involves only observed trade shares, incomes and the trade elasticity, so that preference shifters, endowments and trade costs never need to be estimated. Starting from the Armington model, the chapter adds, one at a time, alternative market structures (perfect competition, monopolistic competition with free entry, firm heterogeneity as in Melitz with Pareto productivity), multiple sectors, tradable intermediate goods and multiple factors, and for each variant it derives the gravity equation and the formula for the gains from trade, defined as the absolute value of the percentage change in real income from moving to autarky. All models are calibrated to the same data, the World Input-Output Database (WIOD) for 2008 with 27 EU countries and 13 other major countries, and to the same trade elasticities, so differences in predictions come from different counterfactual equilibria and not from different fits of the initial equilibrium.

The headline numbers are as follows. In the one-sector model the gains from trade average 4.4 percent and are 1.8 percent for the United States. Multiple sectors with Cobb-Douglas upper-level preferences raise the average to about 15 percent, tradable intermediate goods to about 27 percent, and monopolistic competition with intermediates to 32 percent (Krugman) and 40 percent (Melitz). For trade policy, the optimal unilateral tariff in the Armington model is close to 20 percent and its gains are small (0.3 percent for the United States), while a worldwide 40 percent tariff lowers real consumption by 2.3 percent on average in the one-sector model and by 7.0 percent in a model with intermediates and firm heterogeneity.

Armington Model and the Gravity Equation

There are i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,ni=1,…,n countries, each endowed with QiQ_iQi​ units of a distinct good. The representative agent in country jjj has CES preferences:

Cj=(∑i=1nψij(1−σ)/σCij(σ−1)/σ)σ/(σ−1)(1)C_j=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{ij}^{(1-\sigma)/\sigma}C_{ij}^{(\sigma-1)/\sigma}\right)^{\sigma/(\sigma-1)} \tag{1}Cj​=(i=1∑n​ψij(1−σ)/σ​Cij(σ−1)/σ​)σ/(σ−1)(1)

where CijC_{ij}Cij​ is the demand for good iii in country jjj, ψij>0\psi_{ij}>0ψij​>0 is a preference parameter and σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 is the elasticity of substitution. The associated consumer price index is Pj=(∑i=1nψij1−σPij1−σ)1/(1−σ)P_j=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\right)^{1/(1-\sigma)}Pj​=(∑i=1n​ψij1−σ​Pij1−σ​)1/(1−σ). Trade is subject to iceberg trade costs: selling one unit in jjj requires shipping τij≥1\tau_{ij}\geq1τij​≥1 units from iii, with τii=1\tau_{ii}=1τii​=1. No arbitrage gives Pij=τijPiiP_{ij}=\tau_{ij}P_{ii}Pij​=τij​Pii​, and since the domestic price equals income per unit of endowment, Pii=Yi/QiP_{ii}=Y_i/Q_iPii​=Yi​/Qi​:

Pij=YiτijQi(2)P_{ij}=\frac{Y_i\tau_{ij}}{Q_i} \tag{2}Pij​=Qi​Yi​τij​​(2)

Let XijX_{ij}Xij​ be the value of country jjj's imports from iii and Ej≡∑i=1nXijE_j\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{ij}Ej​≡∑i=1n​Xij​ total expenditure. CES demand gives Xij=(ψijPij/Pj)1−σEjX_{ij}=\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}/P_j\right)^{1-\sigma}E_jXij​=(ψij​Pij​/Pj​)1−σEj​. Define χij≡(Qi/ψij)σ−1\chi_{ij}\equiv\left(Q_i/\psi_{ij}\right)^{\sigma-1}χij​≡(Qi​/ψij​)σ−1 and the trade elasticity ε≡∂ln⁡(Xij/Xjj)/∂ln⁡τij\varepsilon\equiv\partial\ln\left(X_{ij}/X_{jj}\right)/\partial\ln\tau_{ij}ε≡∂ln(Xij​/Xjj​)/∂lnτij​ in absolute value, holding incomes fixed, which here equals σ−1\sigma-1σ−1. Then trade flows satisfy the gravity equation:

Xij=(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljEj(3)X_{ij}=\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}E_j \tag{3}Xij​=∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Ej​(3)

In a competitive equilibrium, budget balance Yi=EiY_i=E_iYi​=Ei​ and goods market clearing Yi=∑j=1nXijY_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Yi​=∑j=1n​Xij​ imply:

Yi=∑j=1n(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljYj(4)Y_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}Y_j \tag{4}Yi​=j=1∑n​∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Yj​(4)

This is a system of nnn equations in the nnn income levels, one of which is redundant by Walras' law, so incomes are determined up to a normalization.

Welfare: Two Sufficient Statistics

Welfare changes are percentage changes in real consumption Cj≡Ej/PjC_j\equiv E_j/P_jCj​≡Ej​/Pj​, which equal the equivalent variation of a shock as a share of initial expenditure. Let λij≡Xij/Ej\lambda_{ij}\equiv X_{ij}/E_jλij​≡Xij​/Ej​ be the share of country jjj's expenditure on goods from iii. For an infinitesimal change in trade costs, Shephard's lemma gives dln⁡Pj=∑i=1nλijdln⁡Pijd\ln P_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{ij}d\ln P_{ij}dlnPj​=∑i=1n​λij​dlnPij​. With CES demand, relative expenditure on imports versus domestic goods moves with relative prices with elasticity 1−σ1-\sigma1−σ, so import prices can be eliminated in favor of the domestic share:

dln⁡Pj=dln⁡Pjj−dln⁡λjj1−σ(5)d\ln P_j=d\ln P_{jj}-\frac{d\ln\lambda_{jj}}{1-\sigma} \tag{5}dlnPj​=dlnPjj​−1−σdlnλjj​​(5)

Hence dln⁡Cj=(dln⁡Ej−dln⁡Pjj)+dln⁡λjj/(1−σ)d\ln C_j=\left(d\ln E_j-d\ln P_{jj}\right)+d\ln\lambda_{jj}/(1-\sigma)dlnCj​=(dlnEj​−dlnPjj​)+dlnλjj​/(1−σ). In the Armington model the first term is zero because Ej=YjE_j=Y_jEj​=Yj​ and Pjj=Yj/QjP_{jj}=Y_j/Q_jPjj​=Yj​/Qj​, so dln⁡Cj=−dln⁡λjj/εd\ln C_j=-d\ln\lambda_{jj}/\varepsilondlnCj​=−dlnλjj​/ε. Let v^≡v′/v\hat{v}\equiv v'/vv^≡v′/v denote the proportional change of any variable vvv between the initial and the counterfactual equilibrium. Integrating gives the welfare formula:

C^j=λ^jj−1/ε(6)\hat{C}_j=\hat{\lambda}_{jj}^{-1/\varepsilon} \tag{6}C^j​=λ^jj−1/ε​(6)

For any change in trade costs, foreign preferences or foreign endowments, the change in the domestic expenditure share λjj\lambda_{jj}λjj​ and the trade elasticity ε\varepsilonε are sufficient to infer the welfare change. The intuition is that the domestic share reveals the change in the relative price of imports, which is the terms-of-trade change, and ε\varepsilonε converts quantities into prices.

Exact Hat Algebra

To predict λ^jj\hat{\lambda}_{jj}λ^jj​ for a given shock from τij\tau_{ij}τij​ to τij′\tau'_{ij}τij′​, write the gravity equation in the initial and the counterfactual equilibrium and take ratios:

λ^ij=(Y^iτ^ij)−ε∑l=1nλlj(Y^lτ^lj)−ε(7)\hat{\lambda}_{ij}=\frac{\left(\hat{Y}_i\hat{\tau}_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\lambda_{lj}\left(\hat{Y}_l\hat{\tau}_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}} \tag{7}λ^ij​=∑l=1n​λlj​(Y^l​τ^lj​)−ε(Y^i​τ^ij​)−ε​(7)

Substituting into the counterfactual market clearing condition Yj′=∑i=1nλji′Yi′Y'_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda'_{ji}Y'_iYj′​=∑i=1n​λji′​Yi′​ gives a system in the income changes alone:

Y^jYj=∑i=1nλji(Y^jτ^ji)−εY^iYi∑l=1nλli(Y^lτ^li)−ε(8)\hat{Y}_jY_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{ji}\left(\hat{Y}_j\hat{\tau}_{ji}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\hat{Y}_iY_i}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\lambda_{li}\left(\hat{Y}_l\hat{\tau}_{li}\right)^{-\varepsilon}} \tag{8}Y^j​Yj​=i=1∑n​∑l=1n​λli​(Y^l​τ^li​)−ελji​(Y^j​τ^ji​)−εY^i​Yi​​(8)

The structural parameters τij\tau_{ij}τij​ and χij\chi_{ij}χij​ do not appear. The only inputs are the initial shares λij\lambda_{ij}λij​, the initial incomes YiY_iYi​ and ε\varepsilonε; the solution Y^i\hat{Y}_iY^i​ (up to normalization) delivers λ^ij\hat{\lambda}_{ij}λ^ij​ and then C^j\hat{C}_jC^j​. The method is "exact" because it holds for arbitrarily large shocks, unlike local hat algebra in the tradition of Jones. For the move to autarky, τij′=+∞\tau'_{ij}=+\inftyτij′​=+∞ for all i≠ji\neq ji=j, no system needs to be solved: λjj′=1\lambda'_{jj}=1λjj′​=1, so λ^jj=1/λjj\hat{\lambda}_{jj}=1/\lambda_{jj}λ^jj​=1/λjj​, and the gains from trade are:

Gj=1−λjj1/ε(9)G_j=1-\lambda_{jj}^{1/\varepsilon} \tag{9}Gj​=1−λjj1/ε​(9)

The trade elasticity can be estimated from the log of the gravity equation with exporter and importer fixed effects:

ln⁡Xij=δiX+δjM−εln⁡τij+δij(10)\ln X_{ij}=\delta^X_i+\delta^M_j-\varepsilon\ln\tau_{ij}+\delta_{ij} \tag{10}lnXij​=δiX​+δjM​−εlnτij​+δij​(10)

where δiX≡−εln⁡Yi\delta^X_i\equiv-\varepsilon\ln Y_iδiX​≡−εlnYi​, δjM\delta^M_jδjM​ absorbs ln⁡Ej\ln E_jlnEj​ and the denominator of the gravity equation, and δij≡ln⁡χij\delta_{ij}\equiv\ln\chi_{ij}δij​≡lnχij​ is treated as a preference shock orthogonal to ln⁡τij\ln\tau_{ij}lnτij​. The chapter sets ε=5\varepsilon=5ε=5 in one-sector exercises and measures λjj\lambda_{jj}λjj​ as one minus total imports over total expenditure.

Many Models, One Equation

The gravity equation also holds under perfect competition as in Eaton and Kortum (2002), Bertrand competition as in Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003), monopolistic competition with homogeneous firms as in Krugman (1980), and monopolistic competition with heterogeneous firms as in Melitz (2003) with Pareto productivity (Chaney 2008). In these models the representative agent has CES preferences over a continuum of varieties ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omegaω∈Ω, trade is balanced, and each variety is bought from one country, so the Armington utility function and price index still hold with ψij=1\psi_{ij}=1ψij​=1 and Pij=(∫ω∈Ωijpj(ω)1−σdω)1/(1−σ)P_{ij}=\left(\int_{\omega\in\Omega_{ij}}p_j(\omega)^{1-\sigma}d\omega\right)^{1/(1-\sigma)}Pij​=(∫ω∈Ωij​​pj​(ω)1−σdω)1/(1−σ). The difference is that the set Ωij\Omega_{ij}Ωij​ of goods that jjj buys from iii is endogenous. The chapter summarizes all of these models by one reduced-form price equation:

Pij=τijcip×((Ejcijx)δ1−στijcipPj)η×(Ricie)δ1−σ×ξij(11)P_{ij}=\tau_{ij}c^p_i\times\left(\left(\frac{E_j}{c^x_{ij}}\right)^{\frac{\delta}{1-\sigma}}\frac{\tau_{ij}c^p_i}{P_j}\right)^{\eta}\times\left(\frac{R_i}{c^e_i}\right)^{\frac{\delta}{1-\sigma}}\times\xi_{ij} \tag{11}Pij​=τij​cip​×​(cijx​Ej​​)1−σδ​Pj​τij​cip​​​η×(cie​Ri​​)1−σδ​×ξij​(11)

where cipc^p_icip​, cijxc^x_{ij}cijx​ and ciec^e_icie​ capture how input prices affect variable production costs, fixed exporting costs and fixed entry costs, Ri≡∑j=1nXijR_i\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Ri​≡∑j=1n​Xij​ is total revenue, and ξij>0\xi_{ij}>0ξij​>0 collects structural parameters other than τij\tau_{ij}τij​. The first term is the intensive margin, the only one active in the Armington model, where cip=Yic^p_i=Y_icip​=Yi​, δ=0\delta=0δ=0 and η=0\eta=0η=0. The second term is the extensive margin due to selection: when firms from iii are less competitive in jjj, fewer of them serve that market. The third term is the extensive margin due to entry: where entry is more profitable, more varieties are created, which lowers the price index with elasticity 1/(σ−1)1/(\sigma-1)1/(σ−1). The dummy δ\deltaδ equals one under monopolistic competition with free entry and zero under perfect or Bertrand competition. The parameter η≥0\eta\geq0η≥0 measures heterogeneity: η=0\eta=0η=0 in Krugman (1980), where all firms export, and η≡(θσ−1)(1+1−σθ)\eta\equiv\left(\frac{\theta}{\sigma-1}\right)\left(1+\frac{1-\sigma}{\theta}\right)η≡(σ−1θ​)(1+θ1−σ​) in the other models, where θ>σ−1\theta>\sigma-1θ>σ−1 is the shape parameter of the productivity distribution (Frechet under perfect and Bertrand competition, Pareto under monopolistic competition).

One Sector: Equivalence Across Market Structures

In one-sector models, all factors are used in the same proportions in production, exporting and entry, cip=ciix=cie=Yic^p_i=c^x_{ii}=c^e_i=Y_icip​=ciix​=cie​=Yi​, and trade in goods is balanced, Ri=YiR_i=Y_iRi​=Yi​. The entry term then drops out, since Ri/cie=1R_i/c^e_i=1Ri​/cie​=1, and the gravity equation generalizes to:

Xij=(Yiτij)−ε(cijx)−δηχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−ε(cljx)−δηχljEj(12)X_{ij}=\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\left(c^x_{ij}\right)^{-\delta\eta}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\left(c^x_{lj}\right)^{-\delta\eta}\chi_{lj}}E_j \tag{12}Xij​=∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−ε(cljx​)−δηχlj​(Yi​τij​)−ε(cijx​)−δηχij​​Ej​(12)

with ε=(1+η)(σ−1)\varepsilon=(1+\eta)(\sigma-1)ε=(1+η)(σ−1) and χij≡ξij1−σ\chi_{ij}\equiv\xi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}χij​≡ξij1−σ​. With selection the trade elasticity is no longer σ−1\sigma-1σ−1, because trade costs move both the prices of existing varieties and the set of varieties traded, but it is still recovered from the same gravity regression. For welfare, the relation between dln⁡Pjd\ln P_jdlnPj​, dln⁡Pjjd\ln P_{jj}dlnPjj​ and dln⁡λjjd\ln\lambda_{jj}dlnλjj​ still holds by CES, but dln⁡Ej−dln⁡Pjjd\ln E_j-d\ln P_{jj}dlnEj​−dlnPjj​ is no longer zero. From the price equation with Ej=YjE_j=Y_jEj​=Yj​ and cjjx=Yjc^x_{jj}=Y_jcjjx​=Yj​, dln⁡Pjj=(1+η)dln⁡Yj−ηdln⁡Pjd\ln P_{jj}=(1+\eta)d\ln Y_j-\eta d\ln P_jdlnPjj​=(1+η)dlnYj​−ηdlnPj​, so:

dln⁡Ej−dln⁡Pjj=−ηη+1×dln⁡λjj1−σ(13)d\ln E_j-d\ln P_{jj}=-\frac{\eta}{\eta+1}\times\frac{d\ln\lambda_{jj}}{1-\sigma} \tag{13}dlnEj​−dlnPjj​=−η+1η​×1−σdlnλjj​​(13)

A positive terms-of-trade shock lowers the profitability of domestic firms at home, reduces the number of domestically produced goods and raises the price index of domestic goods. Adding the two effects gives dln⁡Cj=−dln⁡λjj/εd\ln C_j=-d\ln\lambda_{jj}/\varepsilondlnCj​=−dlnλjj​/ε again. This is the result of Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012): conditional on λjj\lambda_{jj}λjj​ and ε\varepsilonε, selection and scale effects do not change the welfare formula or the gains from trade Gj=1−λjj1/εG_j=1-\lambda_{jj}^{1/\varepsilon}Gj​=1−λjj1/ε​. New varieties may well matter for welfare; the point is that their effect is already revealed by aggregate trade flows. If, in addition, fixed exporting costs are paid in the destination country, cijx=cjxc^x_{ij}=c^x_jcijx​=cjx​, then cijxc^x_{ij}cijx​ cancels from the gravity equation and the exact hat algebra and all counterfactual predictions coincide with those of the Armington model. If fixed exporting costs are paid partly in the origin country, the Melitz model predicts different changes in relative wages and hence in λjj\lambda_{jj}λjj​ for a given finite shock, with the move to autarky as a notable exception.

Three lessons follow. First, δs\delta_sδs​ appears, so perfect and monopolistic competition now differ through scale effects: a country that is a net exporter in sectors with strong scale effects (high δs/εs\delta_s/\varepsilon_sδs​/εs​, low ej,s/rj,se_{j,s}/r_{j,s}ej,s​/rj,s​) gains more than under perfect competition, and a country with a comparative disadvantage in those sectors gains less. Second, ηs\eta_sηs​ does not appear, so conditional on trade flows and trade elasticities, models with and without firm heterogeneity predict the same gains. Third, multi-sector gains are much larger than one-sector gains, in part because of the Cobb-Douglas assumption: if the price of one good becomes arbitrarily large in autarky, either because λjj,s\lambda_{jj,s}λjj,s​ is close to zero or because εs\varepsilon_sεs​ is close to zero, the gains from trade are infinite.

Tradable Intermediate Goods

Intermediate goods are introduced by assuming that, in each sector, they are produced with the same CES aggregator as the composite good for final consumption, so that Pj,sP_{j,s}Pj,s​ is the price of sector sss goods for both final consumption and production. Unit costs become:

Data and Calibration

All exercises use WIOD for 2008: 27 EU countries, 13 other major countries and a rest of the world, with 31 sectors. Sector-level trade elasticities for agriculture and manufacturing are from Caliendo and Parro (2010), who estimate them from a triple difference of the sector-level gravity equation using tariff variation; they average about 8, and the elasticity for service sectors is set to 5. Service sectors are always perfectly competitive. In the monopolistic competition columns, δs=1\delta_s=1δs​=1 for agriculture and manufacturing, with ηs=0\eta_s=0ηs​=0 (Krugman) or ηs=0.65\eta_s=0.65ηs​=0.65 (Melitz), the value implied by ε=4.58\varepsilon=4.58ε=4.58 and σ=3.8\sigma=3.8σ=3.8 in Balistreri, Hillberry and Rutherford (2011). With true input shares αj,ks\alpha_{j,ks}αj,ks​ the adjusted Leontief inverse has negative elements under monopolistic competition, so the gains are not finite; the chapter therefore uses the alternative shares αj,ks∗\alpha^*_{j,ks}αj,ks∗​, which assume that all sectors allocate intermediate spending in the same proportions Ej,k/EjE_{j,k}/E_jEj,k​/Ej​. For the tariff exercises the data are modified so that trade is balanced country by country.

Results: Gains from Trade

  • One sector: with ε=5\varepsilon=5ε=5 the gains average 4.4 percent. They are below 2 percent for Brazil (1.5), Japan (1.7) and the United States (1.8), and largest for Slovakia (7.6), Ireland (8.0) and Hungary (8.1).

  • Multiple sectors, no intermediates: the average more than triples to 15.3 percent under perfect competition and is 14.0 percent under monopolistic competition. Belgium goes from 7.5 to 32.7 percent, Canada from 3.8 to 17.4 percent and the United States to 4.4 percent. There is no systematic ranking of the two market structures: Germany rises from 12.7 to 17.6 percent with monopolistic competition, while Greece falls from 16.3 to 4.7 percent.

  • Intermediates, perfect competition: the average is 26.9 percent with the true input shares and 27.1 percent with the alternative shares. The United States rises to 8.3 percent and Japan to 4.6 percent, about two and three times the values without intermediates.

  • Intermediates, monopolistic competition: the average is 32.3 percent in the Krugman case and 40.0 percent in the Melitz case; the United States gains 8.6 and 10.3 percent and China 28.0 and 77.9 percent. The Melitz numbers are higher because, for a given εs\varepsilon_sεs​, ηs=0.65\eta_s=0.65ηs​=0.65 implies a lower σs\sigma_sσs​ (2.9 instead of 4.2 when εs=3.2\varepsilon_s=3.2εs​=3.2) and hence a stronger love of variety. With ηs=1.5\eta_s=1.5ηs​=1.5, as estimated from firm-level data, the gains would not be finite for any country.

  • Sensitivity: treating physical capital as a tradable intermediate raises the average with perfect competition from 26.9 to 34.6 percent. Making all factors sector-specific in the multi-factor model raises the average from 15.3 to 17.2 percent.

Results: Tariffs

  • Unilateral tariff, Armington: starting from zero tariffs with ε=5\varepsilon=5ε=5, the welfare-maximizing uniform tariff is around 20 percent for the United States, France, Portugal and Ireland. The gains at the optimum are modest, from 0.3 percent for the United States to 1.3 percent for Ireland, and tariffs up to about 50 percent still raise real consumption relative to free trade.

  • United States tariff of 40 percent: in the one-sector model the United States gains 0.21 percent and other countries lose 0.2 percent on average, with Canada (−1.2-1.2−1.2 percent) and Mexico (−1.1-1.1−1.1 percent) the exceptions. With multiple sectors the United States gains 0.41 percent, and with intermediates 0.63 percent, while the average loss abroad rises from 0.14 to 0.33 percent and Canada loses 2.3 percent.

  • Worldwide tariff of 40 percent: in the one-sector model the average loss is 2.3 percent, from 0.8 percent for the United States to 4.4 percent for Ireland. With multiple sectors the average loss falls to 1.4 percent, so the autarky ranking of models does not extrapolate to finite tariffs, and with intermediates it rises to 3.4 percent.

  • Market structure: on a coarser dataset with 10 regions and 16 sectors, the average loss from the worldwide tariff without intermediates is 1.1 percent under perfect competition, 1.4 percent under Krugman and 1.2 percent under Melitz. With intermediates it is 2.5, 5.3 and 7.0 percent, and for China 2.5, 13.4 and 20.3 percent. Fixed exporting costs are paid in the exporting country and tariffs are imposed before markups.

  • Tariff dispersion: if United States tariffs are 20 or 60 percent across sectors with a mean of 40 percent, the United States gain falls from 0.41 to 0.26 percent and losses abroad shrink. The uniform tariff that yields the same welfare, the Trade Restrictiveness Index of Anderson and Neary (2005), is not unique: both 8.5 and 69 percent do.

  • Trade imbalances: welfare effects of the worldwide tariff under the two deficit rules have a correlation of 0.86 with each other and only 0.57 with the balanced-trade results.

Which Elasticities Matter

The chapter closes by asking how much the numbers depend on elasticities that gravity regressions do not identify. First, replace the Cobb-Douglas upper tier by a CES aggregator over sectors with elasticity γ>0\gamma>0γ>0. Under perfect competition the welfare change is C^j=(∑s=1Sej,s(λ^jj,s−1)(γ−1)/εs)1/(γ−1)\hat{C}_j=\left(\sum_{s=1}^{S}e_{j,s}\left(\hat{\lambda}_{jj,s}^{-1}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\varepsilon_s}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)}C^j​=(∑s=1S​ej,s​(λ^jj,s−1​)(γ−1)/εs​)1/(γ−1) and the gains from trade are:

Gj=1−(∑s=1Sej,s(λjj,s)(γ−1)/εs)1/(γ−1)(31)G_j=1-\left(\sum_{s=1}^{S}e_{j,s}\left(\lambda_{jj,s}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\varepsilon_s}\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)} \tag{31}Gj​=1−(s=1∑S​ej,s​(λjj,s​)(γ−1)/εs​)1/(γ−1)(31)

Average gains fall from 45 percent in the Leontief case γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 to 15 percent at γ=1\gamma=1γ=1 and 3 percent at γ=8\gamma=8γ=8; when εs=γ−1\varepsilon_s=\gamma-1εs​=γ−1 for all sss the one-sector formula returns. Second, in an Armington model in which the domestic good and a composite of imports are combined with elasticity γ\gammaγ while imports from different sources are combined with elasticity σ\sigmaσ, gravity regressions across foreign sources identify σ\sigmaσ, but welfare depends on γ\gammaγ:

dln⁡Cj=dln⁡λjj1−γ(32)d\ln C_j=\frac{d\ln\lambda_{jj}}{1-\gamma} \tag{32}dlnCj​=1−γdlnλjj​​(32)

Only the assumption of symmetric CES lets researchers go from the estimated elasticity to the welfare-relevant one; Head and Ries (2001) and Feenstra et al. (2013) suggest the two are similar. Third, estimates of the trade elasticity itself range widely, from ε=3.60\varepsilon=3.60ε=3.60 to ε=12.86\varepsilon=12.86ε=12.86 in Eaton and Kortum (2002), with 4.12 preferred by Simonovska and Waugh (2011), and sector-level estimates are imprecise: an elasticity near zero in one sector implies infinite gains. Finally, the three elasticities are linked by η=(ε−(σ−1))/(σ−1)\eta=\left(\varepsilon-(\sigma-1)\right)/(\sigma-1)η=(ε−(σ−1))/(σ−1), so under monopolistic competition the calibration of σ\sigmaσ or η\etaη determines the size of scale effects.

This is the primitive of the Armington model: the utility of the representative agent in country jjj, a constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) aggregate of the nnn national goods. CijC_{ij}Cij​ is the quantity of the good of country iii consumed in jjj (first index origin, second index destination), σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 is the elasticity of substitution between goods of different origins, and ψij>0\psi_{ij}>0ψij​>0 is a preference shifter. Because the exponent on ψij\psi_{ij}ψij​ is (1−σ)/σ<0(1-\sigma)/\sigma<0(1−σ)/σ<0, a higher ψij\psi_{ij}ψij​ means that country jjj likes good iii less; ψij\psi_{ij}ψij​ acts exactly like a multiplicative price wedge, which is why it later merges with trade costs and endowments in the shifter χij\chi_{ij}χij​ of equation (3).

Maximizing CjC_jCj​ subject to ∑iPijCij=Ej\sum_iP_{ij}C_{ij}=E_j∑i​Pij​Cij​=Ej​ gives the demand and the price index used throughout the note (the steps are in the derivation of equation (3)):

Cij=ψij1−σ(PijPj)−σCj,Pj=(∑i=1nψij1−σPij1−σ)1/(1−σ),PjCj=EjC_{ij}=\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\left(\frac{P_{ij}}{P_j}\right)^{-\sigma}C_j,\qquad P_j=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\right)^{1/(1-\sigma)},\qquad P_jC_j=E_jCij​=ψij1−σ​(Pj​Pij​​)−σCj​,Pj​=(i=1∑n​ψij1−σ​Pij1−σ​)1/(1−σ),Pj​Cj​=Ej​

The functional form buys three things. First, the utility function is homothetic, so real consumption is Cj=Ej/PjC_j=E_j/P_jCj​=Ej​/Pj​ and welfare changes are changes in real expenditure. Second, relative demand for any two origins depends only on their relative price, with the constant elasticity σ\sigmaσ:

∂ln⁡(Xij/Xjj)∂ln⁡(Pij/Pjj)=1−σ\frac{\partial\ln\left(X_{ij}/X_{jj}\right)}{\partial\ln\left(P_{ij}/P_{jj}\right)}=1-\sigma∂ln(Pij​/Pjj​)∂ln(Xij​/Xjj​)​=1−σ

This single number becomes the trade elasticity ε=σ−1\varepsilon=\sigma-1ε=σ−1 and drives equations (3), (5) and (6). Third, with σ>1\sigma>1σ>1 no good is essential, so autarky utility is finite and the gains from trade in equation (9) are well defined. What the form rules out is any pattern of substitution that differs across pairs of countries, and any difference between the elasticity among foreign sources and the elasticity between domestic and foreign goods; equation (32) shows what happens when that last restriction is relaxed.

The equation combines no arbitrage with the definition of income in an endowment economy. Start with no arbitrage. Delivering one unit of good iii to country jjj requires shipping τij\tau_{ij}τij​ units, each of which could be sold at home at the price PiiP_{ii}Pii​. Competitive traders make zero profits, so

Pij=τijPiiP_{ij}=\tau_{ij}P_{ii}Pij​=τij​Pii​

Next, compute the income of country iii. Its only source of income is the sale of its endowment. The resource constraint says that the quantities shipped, including the part that melts in transit, exhaust the endowment: ∑jτijCij=Qi\sum_j\tau_{ij}C_{ij}=Q_i∑j​τij​Cij​=Qi​. Total sales revenue is therefore

Yi=∑j=1nPijCij=Pii∑j=1nτijCij=PiiQiY_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{ij}C_{ij}=P_{ii}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\tau_{ij}C_{ij}=P_{ii}Q_iYi​=j=1∑n​Pij​Cij​=Pii​j=1∑n​τij​Cij​=Pii​Qi​

where the second equality uses no arbitrage. Hence Pii=Yi/QiP_{ii}=Y_i/Q_iPii​=Yi​/Qi​: the domestic price is income per unit of endowment. Substituting back into the no-arbitrage condition,

Pij=τijPii=YiτijQiP_{ij}=\tau_{ij}P_{ii}=\frac{Y_i\tau_{ij}}{Q_i}Pij​=τij​Pii​=Qi​Yi​τij​​

The useful feature is that the unknown price PiiP_{ii}Pii​ has been replaced by income YiY_iYi​, which is observable, and the endowment QiQ_iQi​, which will be absorbed into the shifter χij\chi_{ij}χij​. In the more general models of equation (11) the same role is played by cipc^p_icip​, the price of the input bundle, which in a one-factor model is again proportional to YiY_iYi​.

Step 1, CES demand. The consumer in jjj maximizes the utility function (1) subject to ∑iPijCij=Ej\sum_iP_{ij}C_{ij}=E_j∑i​Pij​Cij​=Ej​. With multiplier μ\muμ on the budget constraint, the first-order condition for CijC_{ij}Cij​ is

ψij(1−σ)/σCij−1/σCj1/σ=μPij⟹Cij=ψij1−σ(μPij)−σCj\psi_{ij}^{(1-\sigma)/\sigma}C_{ij}^{-1/\sigma}C_j^{1/\sigma}=\mu P_{ij}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_{ij}=\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\left(\mu P_{ij}\right)^{-\sigma}C_jψij(1−σ)/σ​Cij−1/σ​Cj1/σ​=μPij​⟹Cij​=ψij1−σ​(μPij​)−σCj​

Substituting this demand back into the utility function (1) and cancelling CjC_jCj​ pins down the multiplier:

1=μ1−σ∑i=1nψij1−σPij1−σ⟹1μ=(∑i=1nψij1−σPij1−σ)1/(1−σ)≡Pj1=\mu^{1-\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{1}{\mu}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\right)^{1/(1-\sigma)}\equiv P_j1=μ1−σi=1∑n​ψij1−σ​Pij1−σ​⟹μ1​=(i=1∑n​ψij1−σ​Pij1−σ​)1/(1−σ)≡Pj​

so that Cij=ψij1−σ(Pij/Pj)−σCjC_{ij}=\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}\left(P_{ij}/P_j\right)^{-\sigma}C_jCij​=ψij1−σ​(Pij​/Pj​)−σCj​ and, summing spending over iii, Ej=PjCjE_j=P_jC_jEj​=Pj​Cj​.

Step 2, the value of bilateral trade. Multiply demand by the price:

Xij≡PijCij=ψij1−σPij1−σPjσ−1(PjCj)=(ψijPijPj)1−σEj=(ψijPij)1−σ∑l=1n(ψljPlj)1−σEjX_{ij}\equiv P_{ij}C_{ij}=\psi_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_{ij}^{1-\sigma}P_j^{\sigma-1}\left(P_jC_j\right)=\left(\frac{\psi_{ij}P_{ij}}{P_j}\right)^{1-\sigma}E_j=\frac{\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}\right)^{1-\sigma}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(\psi_{lj}P_{lj}\right)^{1-\sigma}}E_jXij​≡Pij​Cij​=ψij1−σ​Pij1−σ​Pjσ−1​(Pj​Cj​)=(Pj​ψij​Pij​​)1−σEj​=∑l=1n​(ψlj​Plj​)1−σ(ψij​Pij​)1−σ​Ej​

Step 3, substitute the price equation (2), Pij=Yiτij/QiP_{ij}=Y_i\tau_{ij}/Q_iPij​=Yi​τij​/Qi​:

(ψijPij)1−σ=(Yiτij)1−σ(Qiψij)σ−1=(Yiτij)−εχij,ε≡σ−1,χij≡(Qiψij)σ−1\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}\right)^{1-\sigma}=\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{1-\sigma}\left(\frac{Q_i}{\psi_{ij}}\right)^{\sigma-1}=\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij},\qquad\varepsilon\equiv\sigma-1,\quad\chi_{ij}\equiv\left(\frac{Q_i}{\psi_{ij}}\right)^{\sigma-1}(ψij​Pij​)1−σ=(Yi​τij​)1−σ(ψij​Qi​​)σ−1=(Yi​τij​)−εχij​,ε≡σ−1,χij​≡(ψij​Qi​​)σ−1

Using this in the numerator and in every term of the denominator gives the gravity equation:

Xij=(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljEjX_{ij}=\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}E_jXij​=∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Ej​

Step 4, check that ε\varepsilonε is the trade elasticity. Taking the ratio of imports from iii to domestic sales removes the denominator and EjE_jEj​:

ln⁡XijXjj=−εln⁡τij−εln⁡YiYj+ln⁡χijχjj,∂ln⁡(Xij/Xjj)∂ln⁡τij=−ε=−(σ−1)\ln\frac{X_{ij}}{X_{jj}}=-\varepsilon\ln\tau_{ij}-\varepsilon\ln\frac{Y_i}{Y_j}+\ln\frac{\chi_{ij}}{\chi_{jj}},\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\left(X_{ij}/X_{jj}\right)}{\partial\ln\tau_{ij}}=-\varepsilon=-(\sigma-1)lnXjj​Xij​​=−εlnτij​−εlnYj​Yi​​+lnχjj​χij​​,∂lnτij​∂ln(Xij​/Xjj​)​=−ε=−(σ−1)

holding incomes fixed and using τjj=1\tau_{jj}=1τjj​=1. The equation has the gravity form: bilateral trade rises with the size of the importer (EjE_jEj​), falls with the bilateral cost τij\tau_{ij}τij​ and depends on the exporter through YiY_iYi​, where a higher YiY_iYi​ for a given endowment means a more expensive good; the denominator is the importer's "multilateral resistance", equal to Pj1−σP_j^{1-\sigma}Pj1−σ​.

A competitive equilibrium requires two conditions for every country. Budget balance: the representative agent spends its income, Ei=YiE_i=Y_iEi​=Yi​ (there are no transfers or deficits). Goods market clearing: the income of country iii, which by the derivation of equation (2) equals the value of its sales, is the sum of what all countries spend on its good:

Yi=∑j=1nXijY_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{ij}Yi​=j=1∑n​Xij​

Substitute the gravity equation (3) for XijX_{ij}Xij​ and then budget balance Ej=YjE_j=Y_jEj​=Yj​:

Yi=∑j=1n(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljEj=∑j=1n(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljYjY_i=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}E_j=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}Y_jYi​=j=1∑n​∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Ej​=j=1∑n​∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Yj​

This is the target. Two properties explain why incomes are determined only up to a normalization. First, Walras' law: summing the right-hand side over iii and exchanging the order of summation, the shares add up to one for every jjj, so

∑i=1n∑j=1n(Yiτij)−εχij∑l=1n(Ylτlj)−εχljYj=∑j=1nYj\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\left(Y_i\tau_{ij}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{ij}}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\left(Y_l\tau_{lj}\right)^{-\varepsilon}\chi_{lj}}Y_j=\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_ji=1∑n​j=1∑n​∑l=1n​(Yl​τlj​)−εχlj​(Yi​τij​)−εχij​​Yj​=j=1∑n​Yj​

which equals the sum of the left-hand sides identically. One of the nnn equations is therefore implied by the other n−1n-1n−1. Second, homogeneity: multiplying all incomes by a common factor leaves every share unchanged (numerator and denominator are both scaled by the same power) and scales both sides proportionally. Only relative incomes, that is relative prices of the national goods, are determined; one income is chosen as the numeraire.

Step 1, the price index responds to prices in proportion to expenditure shares. Differentiate ln⁡Pj=11−σln⁡∑i(ψijPij)1−σ\ln P_j=\frac{1}{1-\sigma}\ln\sum_i\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}\right)^{1-\sigma}lnPj​=1−σ1​ln∑i​(ψij​Pij​)1−σ, holding preferences fixed:

dln⁡Pj=∑i=1n(ψijPij)1−σ∑l(ψljPlj)1−σdln⁡Pij=∑i=1nλij dln⁡Pijd\ln P_j=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}\right)^{1-\sigma}}{\sum_{l}\left(\psi_{lj}P_{lj}\right)^{1-\sigma}}d\ln P_{ij}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{ij}\,d\ln P_{ij}dlnPj​=i=1∑n​∑l​(ψlj​Plj​)1−σ(ψij​Pij​)1−σ​dlnPij​=i=1∑n​λij​dlnPij​

because λij=Xij/Ej=(ψijPij/Pj)1−σ\lambda_{ij}=X_{ij}/E_j=\left(\psi_{ij}P_{ij}/P_j\right)^{1-\sigma}λij​=Xij​/Ej​=(ψij​Pij​/Pj​)1−σ by Step 2 of the derivation of equation (3). This is Shephard's lemma applied to the unit expenditure function.

Step 2, shares reveal relative prices. From the same expression for λij\lambda_{ij}λij​, the ratio of two shares depends only on the ratio of the two prices:

λijλjj=(ψijPijψjjPjj)1−σ⟹dln⁡Pij=dln⁡Pjj+dln⁡λij−dln⁡λjj1−σ\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\lambda_{jj}}=\left(\frac{\psi_{ij}P_{ij}}{\psi_{jj}P_{jj}}\right)^{1-\sigma}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d\ln P_{ij}=d\ln P_{jj}+\frac{d\ln\lambda_{ij}-d\ln\lambda_{jj}}{1-\sigma}λjj​λij​​=(ψjj​Pjj​ψij​Pij​​)1−σ⟹dlnPij​=dlnPjj​+1−σdlnλij​−dlnλjj​​

The result uses only CES demand, so it holds in every model of the note with a CES lower tier. It also holds globally and not only for small changes, since λjj=(ψjjPjj/Pj)1−σ\lambda_{jj}=\left(\psi_{jj}P_{jj}/P_j\right)^{1-\sigma}λjj​=(ψjj​Pjj​/Pj​)1−σ gives Pj=ψjjPjjλjj−1/(1−σ)P_j=\psi_{jj}P_{jj}\lambda_{jj}^{-1/(1-\sigma)}Pj​=ψjj​Pjj​λjj−1/(1−σ)​ directly. The derivation treats ψij\psi_{ij}ψij​ as fixed; shocks to foreign preferences ψij\psi_{ij}ψij​, i≠ji\neq ji=j, are covered by reading ψijPij\psi_{ij}P_{ij}ψij​Pij​ as the effective price, but the home shifter ψjj\psi_{jj}ψjj​ must not change. Economically, a fall in λjj\lambda_{jj}λjj​ signals that imports have become cheaper relative to the domestic good, so the price index falls relative to PjjP_{jj}Pjj​, by more when goods are poor substitutes (low σ\sigmaσ).
